name: Speech in Indian Languages
question: Does the agent hear Hindi, Tamil and Hinglish correctly?
summary: Speech recognition and synthesis for Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and other Indian languages, including callers who switch between them and English mid-sentence. Accuracy differs widely by language, accent and channel: an English-first model that is fine on English can get half the words wrong in Tamil on an 8 kHz phone line. The work is choosing an Indic-tuned recogniser, identifying the language turn by turn, boosting your own vocabulary, turning spoken amounts such as “saadhe teen hazaar” into ₹3,500, and measuring word error rate per language on your own call recordings. Latency and the voice loop itself belong to Realtime Voice Agents; this is about language quality.
useCases: Helplines where callers speak Hindi, Hinglish, Tamil, Bengali and English
Calls that capture amounts, policy numbers, names and dates
Choosing between English-first, multilingual and Indic-tuned speech vendors

steps: Sample and transcribe your own calls, stratified by language, accent and channel
Identify the language on every turn and route to a recogniser tuned for it and for 8 kHz audio
Add custom vocabulary and rules that turn spoken amounts into numbers, then read them back
Report WER per language and amount accuracy, and hand low-confidence turns to a person
pitfalls: Choosing a model on a clean, wideband benchmark instead of your own phone calls
One blended WER that hides a failing Tamil or Bengali slice
Fixing the language at the start of the call when callers switch mid-call
remember: Measure per language on your own calls. Identify each turn, boost your words, read amounts back.
caption: Illustrative: helpline calls at Kavach Bima, a fictional insurer; 45% Hindi, 20% Hinglish, 15% Tamil, 10% Bengali, 10% English.

comparison.scope: Recognition and speech in Indian languages
comparison.best: A good average hiding a failing language

code.text: from kavach.speech import load_turns, identify_language, RECOGNISERS, say   # your wrappers
from kavach.amounts import words_to_rupees, rupees_in_words                  # your rules
lang = identify_language(turn.audio)          # every turn, not once a call
if value is None or hyp.confidence < 0.8:
return None                                   # ask again, then a person
say(f"{rupees_in_words(value, lang)}, sahi hai?", lang=lang)  # read it back

steps.title: Test on your own calls
steps.text: Kavach Bima, a fictional insurer, samples turns from its own recorded calls, at the 8 kHz the phone line delivers, and has people transcribe them. The sample is stratified: 45% Hindi, 20% Hinglish, 15% Tamil, 10% Bengali, 10% English. A clean wideband benchmark would flatter every vendor.

steps.title: Identify the language on every turn
steps.text: Callers switch. A policyholder opens in Tamil, then says the policy number in English. With the language fixed per call, Hinglish WER rose from 18% to 24% even on the Indic-tuned model, and Tamil, Bengali and English got worse too.

steps.title: Route to a recogniser tuned for it
steps.text: Each language goes to a recogniser trained on Indian speech and adapted to 8 kHz audio. The English-first model got 66% of Tamil words wrong; the Indic-tuned one with telephony tuning and per-turn language ID gets 17%, and 16% with the vocabulary added.

steps.title: Boost your own words
steps.text: Plan names and policy terms, such as “Kavach Suraksha Plus”, “grace period” and “revival”, are passed as phrase hints so the recogniser prefers them. They are rare in general speech, so without hints they come out as similar-sounding everyday words.

steps.title: Turn amounts into numbers, then read them back
steps.text: “saadhe teen hazaar” is 3.5 × 1,000 = ₹3,500; “dhai lakh” is ₹2,50,000; “paune chaar hazaar” is ₹3,750. Rules turn the words into a value, and the agent reads it back in the caller’s language before acting. Amount capture rose from 55% to 91%.

steps.title: Score per language, not one average
steps.text: WER and CER are printed per true language, so a good Hindi score cannot hide Tamil. Blended WER fell from 41% to 12%, and calls needing a person from 55% to 17%. Low-confidence amounts are asked again, then handed to a person.

pros: Callers can speak the language, and the mix of languages, they actually use
Amounts, policy numbers and names are captured instead of re-asked
Fewer calls handed to people for being misheard
Per-language scores show exactly where to invest
cons: Needs transcribed recordings in every language you serve
Accuracy still varies by language, accent and line quality
Custom tuning and hosting cost more per minute
Recordings and transcripts are personal data under the DPDP Act
avoidWhen: Nearly all callers speak one well-supported language on good audio (a strong general model is enough)
You cannot collect or label any real calls (start with a narrow pilot and a human fallback)

playgroundGuide.scenario: Kavach Bima, a fictional insurer, runs a helpline where calls are 45% Hindi, 20% Hinglish, 15% Tamil, 10% Bengali and 10% English, over 8 kHz phone lines. Callers ask about premiums, lapsed policies and claims, and say amounts such as “saadhe teen hazaar”. Choose the speech model and three language-quality options, and watch word error rate per language, amounts captured, calls needing a person and cost per minute.
controls: Choose the speech model: English-first global, multilingual general, or Indic-tuned.
Toggle identifying the language on every turn, and custom vocabulary for policy terms and amounts.
Toggle fine-tuning for 8 kHz telephony audio, or load a scenario.

presets.name: English-first, language fixed per call

presets.name: Multilingual general, per-turn language ID
presets.expect: Blended WER 22%, Tamil 30%. 67% of amounts right, 35% need a person, ₹6.49 a minute.

presets.name: Indic-tuned, language fixed per call
presets.expect: Blended WER 19%, but Hinglish 24% and Tamil 25%. 69% of amounts right, 31% need a person, ₹6.27 a minute.

presets.name: Indic-tuned with everything on
presets.expect: Blended WER 12%, Tamil 16%. 91% of amounts right, 17% need a person, ₹4.99 a minute, despite a ₹2.90 speech stack.

missions.text: Capture at least 90% of amounts exactly with no more than 20% of calls going to a person.
missions.hint: It needs the Indic-tuned model, per-turn language ID, custom vocabulary and telephony tuning together.

missions.text: Bring Tamil WER down to 20% or less.
missions.hint: An Indic-tuned model plus 8 kHz telephony tuning, with language ID or vocabulary on.

missions.text: Show that even the Indic-tuned model mishears Hinglish (over 20% WER) when the language is fixed per call.
missions.hint: Choose Indic-tuned, switch off per-turn language ID and leave telephony tuning off.

goals: Explain why WER must be measured per language on your own phone calls
Explain how per-turn language ID, custom vocabulary and amount rules raise accuracy on what matters
Weigh a costlier Indic-tuned stack against the people it saves

practice.scenario: Kavach Bima, a fictional insurer, answers policy and premium calls in Hindi, Hinglish, Tamil, Bengali and English over 8 kHz phone lines. Its first speech model was English-first: fine on English, but it got 66% of Tamil words wrong and captured only 55% of spoken amounts such as “saadhe teen hazaar”. After testing vendors on its own transcribed calls, it moved to an Indic-tuned recogniser adapted to phone audio, identified the language on every turn, boosted plan names and policy terms, and read amounts back. Blended word error rate fell from 41% to 12%, and calls handed to a person from 55% to 17%.

industries.use: Premium, lapse and claim-status calls in Hindi, Tamil and Bengali
EMI and collections calls where amounts and dates must be captured exactly
Appointment and pharmacy lines where medicine names and dosages need custom vocabulary

practice.analogy: A switchboard operator in Chennai who also takes calls from Kolkata and Lucknow. She notices which language each caller is using, even when it changes mid-sentence, knows the company’s product names by heart, and repeats every amount back before writing it down.

library.name: jiwer
library.what: Computes word error rate (WER) and character error rate (CER) between reference transcripts and a recogniser’s output, so you can score each language slice of your own calls.

practice.note: The recogniser, language identification and read-back are vendor-specific, so they are stubs here; wire them to IndicConformer, Sarvam, Bhashini, Google or Azure as you choose. The amount rules cover common Hindi and Hinglish forms only; extend them for Tamil and Bengali numerals and for your own call data. Normalise case and punctuation the same way on both sides before scoring.

numericDrill.question: Kavach Bima’s calls are 45% Hindi, 20% Hinglish, 15% Tamil, 10% Bengali and 10% English. On its own 8 kHz calls, the Indic-tuned model’s word error rates are 10%, 14%, 16%, 14% and 11%. What is the blended WER, in percent?
numericDrill.answer: 0.45 × 10 + 0.20 × 14 + 0.15 × 16 + 0.10 × 14 + 0.10 × 11 = 4.5 + 2.8 + 2.4 + 1.4 + 1.1 = 12.2%. The blend is a summary only: Tamil at 16% is a third worse than Hindi at 10%, so report every slice.

interview.question: How would you choose a speech-recognition model for an Indian-language helpline?
interview.answer: Sample and transcribe real calls at the channel’s 8 kHz, stratified by language, accent and code-mixing, and score each vendor’s WER and CER per slice, plus accuracy on the things that matter: amounts, policy numbers, names and plan names. Compare English-first, multilingual and Indic-tuned models such as IndicConformer, Sarvam, Bhashini, Google and Azure on that set, and weigh accuracy against cost, hosting and data residency. A clean wideband benchmark or a single blended number is not enough.

interview.question: Callers switch between Hindi, English and Tamil. What changes in the speech pipeline?
interview.answer: Identify the language on every turn, or use a recogniser that handles code-mixing, instead of fixing it at the start of the call. Keep the transcript in a consistent script so downstream steps and scoring agree, boost domain terms with custom vocabulary, turn spoken amounts such as “saadhe teen hazaar” into numbers with rules, read them back in the caller’s language, and hand low-confidence turns to a person.

mistakes.fix: Report WER and CER per language and accent, with the worst slice named
Normalise spoken amounts with rules and read them back before acting

quiz.question: A reference transcript has 20 words. The recogniser makes 2 substitutions, 1 deletion and 1 insertion. What is the word error rate?
Calls are 60% Hindi at 10% WER and 40% Tamil at 20% WER. What is the blended WER?
quiz.explanation: 0.6 × 10 + 0.4 × 20 = 6 + 8 = 14%. The Tamil slice is still twice as bad as Hindi.

quiz.question: Phone audio is sampled at 8 kHz. Up to roughly what frequency does it carry sound?
quiz.explanation: Half the sampling rate (the Nyquist limit): 4 kHz, so consonant detail above it is lost. Wideband models trained on 16 kHz audio do worse on it without adaptation.

quiz.question: A caller says the premium is “saadhe teen hazaar”. What value should be stored?
quiz.explanation: Saadhe adds a half: 3.5 × 1,000 = ₹3,500.

quiz.question: A borrower says the outstanding amount is “paune do lakh”. What is it?
quiz.explanation: Paune means a quarter less: 1.75 × 1,00,000 = ₹1,75,000.

quiz.question: A merchant says the refund was “dhai sau rupaye”. What amount is that?
quiz.explanation: Dhai is 2.5, and sau is 100: 2.5 × 100 = ₹250.

quiz.question: A helpline’s English-first model scores 41% blended WER; an Indic-tuned stack scores 12%. Speech costs ₹2.00 and ₹2.90 a minute, and 55% versus 17% of calls need a person at ₹12 a minute. What is the all-in cost per minute of the Indic-tuned stack?
A telecom helpline takes 20,000 calls a day, and 17% need a person. How many calls a day go to people?
A policyholder presses 1 for Hindi, then answers in Tamil. Hinglish and Tamil WER are much worse than on a test set. What is the likely cause?
options: The language is fixed per call from the menu, not identified per turn
The phone line is too fast
quiz.explanation: Callers switch. Identify the language on every turn, or use a model that handles code-mixing.

quiz.question: A pharmacy helpline’s recogniser keeps turning medicine brand names into ordinary words. What is the cheapest first fix?
options: Switch to a larger language model
Pass the brand names as custom vocabulary or phrase hints
Ask callers to spell every name
quiz.explanation: Rare domain terms need boosting. Custom vocabulary makes the recogniser prefer them.

quiz.question: A vendor quotes 6% WER for Hindi on a public benchmark. Your 8 kHz Hindi calls score 18%. What best explains the gap?
options: Clean wideband benchmark audio differs from noisy, narrowband, code-mixed phone calls
quiz.explanation: Channel, noise, accents and code-mixing all raise error rates. Always test on your own calls.

quiz.question: Why is character error rate (CER) often reported alongside WER for Tamil?
options: Long, agglutinative words turn one small error into a whole wrong word, so CER shows partial correctness
CER is always lower, so it looks better
WER cannot be computed for Tamil
quiz.explanation: A single suffix error makes the whole long word wrong under WER; CER gives credit for the rest.

quiz.question: Reference transcripts write Hinglish in Roman script, but the recogniser outputs Devanagari for Hindi words. What happens to measured WER?
options: It is inflated, because correct words in a different script count as errors
quiz.explanation: Normalise script, case and punctuation the same way on both sides before scoring.

quiz.question: What is Bhashini?
options: India’s government platform for Indian-language speech and translation services
quiz.explanation: Bhashini comes from the National Language Translation Mission and offers speech recognition, synthesis and translation services.

quiz.question: The agent heard “saadhe teen hazaar” but confidence is low. What should it do before acting?
options: Read the value back in the caller’s language and ask for confirmation, then hand over if still unsure
quiz.explanation: Read-back turns a silent error into a quick correction; a person takes over if it is still unclear.

quiz.question: An English text-to-speech voice reads “₹3,500 due on 5/9” to Hindi-speaking callers, who find it confusing. What helps most?
options: Write the amount and date as words in the caller’s language and use a Hindi voice, with a pronunciation lexicon for plan names
quiz.explanation: TTS reads what it is given. Normalise amounts and dates into words for the target language, and use a voice and lexicon for that language.

quiz.question: Which of these belong in an evaluation set for an Indian-language helpline? Choose all that apply.
options: Turns from your own recorded calls at 8 kHz
A quota for each language, including Tamil and Bengali
Turns with amounts, policy numbers and names
quiz.explanation: Evaluate on real channel audio, stratified by language, with the entities that matter. Studio audio flatters every model.

quiz.question: Which steps raise the share of spoken amounts captured exactly? Choose all that apply.
options: Rules that convert saadhe, sava, paune, dhai, hazaar and lakh into numbers
Custom vocabulary for number words and amounts
Reading the amount back for confirmation
quiz.explanation: Normalisation, vocabulary and read-back all work on amounts. A blended WER measures nothing about them.

quiz.question: Hospital helpline recordings are used to evaluate speech models. Which practices fit the DPDP Act and good hygiene? Choose all that apply.
options: Tell callers about recording and its purpose
Redact names, phone and policy numbers from transcripts used for scoring
Keep recordings forever in case they are useful
Restrict who can listen to raw audio
quiz.explanation: Recordings are personal data: give notice, minimise, redact and restrict access. Keeping them indefinitely is not good practice. Educational framing, not legal advice.

quiz.question: An Indic-tuned stack costs ₹0.90 a minute more than an English-first one. Which effects can still make it cheaper overall? Choose all that apply.
options: Fewer repeated questions and shorter calls
Fewer wrong amounts to correct later
quiz.explanation: People cost far more per minute than speech models, so accuracy that avoids handovers, repeats and corrections pays for the premium. Higher WER does the opposite.
